summary: This informational document specifies requirements and a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) of Ethernet VPN (EVPN) and Provider Backbone Bridge EVPN. The framework describes a layered OAM model covering the service layer, network layer, underlying packet switched network transport layer and link layer, but focuses on the service and network layers.

eli5.summary: Keeping a big network healthy means checking it for problems. This document describes what checking tools an Ethernet VPN needs and how to organize those checks layer by layer.

questions: how do i detect faults in evpn
subtitle: Tools and layers for diagnosing and monitoring Ethernet VPN networks.

tldr.problem: Ethernet VPN (EVPN) enables large Layer 2 services across carrier networks, but operators need ways to detect faults, measure performance, and diagnose failures when something goes wrong.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9062 defines a layered OAM framework with tools at the service layer (CFM between customer edge devices), network layer (among PE routers), transport layer (MPLS or IP tunnels), and link layer. It also specifies requirements for fault detection, performance measurement, and interworking between layers.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now systematically monitor and troubleshoot EVPN services, pinpointing whether a fault is on the customer side, in the local edge link, in the provider network, or in the remote edge link.

today: RFC 9062 is an Informational document published in June 2021 that defines the requirements and framework for EVPN OAM. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The framework helps operators monitor and troubleshoot modern Ethernet VPN services.

sections.title: Introduction to EVPN
sections.content:
Ethernet VPN (EVPN) is a service that lets enterprises connect Ethernet segments at multiple sites over a carrier network. It uses BGP to advertise which devices are reachable and MPLS to tunnel traffic between provider edge (PE) routers. EVPN is more scalable than older approaches because it avoids flooding unknown MAC addresses across the entire network.

However, when something fails—a link goes down, a device stops responding, or traffic is misrouted—the operator needs a way to find the problem quickly. RFC 9062 defines the requirements and framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) of EVPN and PBB-EVPN services.
sections.eli5: EVPN is a way to carry customer Ethernet traffic through a carrier network using smart routing. When it breaks, you need tools to figure out what went wrong. This document describes those tools.

sections.title: The Layered OAM Model
sections.content:
OAM tools operate at four layers, each with different visibility and purpose.

Service OAM runs end to end between customer edge devices, using Ethernet Connectivity Fault Management (CFM). It is visible to the customer and the PE routers but not to provider interior (P) routers. Service OAM shows whether the emulated Ethernet service is working end to end.

Network OAM operates between PE routers and checks that the MPLS label-switched paths and multicast tunnels are functioning. It is invisible to P routers and customer devices. Network OAM verifies unicast and multicast paths, Designated Forwarder filtering, and split-horizon filtering.

Transport OAM uses MPLS, ICMP, or BFD mechanisms to verify the underlying IP or MPLS network. It operates between all routers (PEs and Ps) and is independent of the Ethernet service layer.

Link OAM checks individual physical links using technology-specific tools (Ethernet Link OAM for Ethernet links, for example).

These layers form a stack: Service OAM at the top, Network OAM below it, Transport OAM below that, and Link OAM at the bottom. Alarms from lower layers can propagate upward to inform higher layers about failures.
sections.eli5: Think of OAM as organized in layers. At the top is the customer's Ethernet layer. Below that is the provider's Ethernet service layer. Below that is the tunneling layer. At the bottom is the physical link layer. Each layer has its own health checks.

sections.title: Fault Detection and Isolation
sections.content:
Proactive fault detection runs continuously. Both Service OAM and Network OAM send periodic keep-alive messages (Continuity Check Messages) to detect when a path or endpoint goes down. These can be run per flow (for specific traffic) or on representative paths (to detect node failures).

Defect indication signals failures in two directions. Forward Defect Indication (FDI) is sent away from the failure and is useful for alarm suppression. Reverse Defect Indication (RDI) is sent back toward the source when a loss of continuity is detected, allowing a network manager to diagnose the problem from a single endpoint.

On-demand fault management is triggered manually by an operator. Connectivity verification messages can carry test payloads to find Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) problems or packet corruption. Fault isolation narrows down the problem to a specific port, link, or node.

Because MPLS/IP networks can have asymmetric routes (forward and reverse paths differ), fault isolation must run in both directions to cover all scenarios.
sections.eli5: There are two types of checks: ones that run all the time to warn of problems, and ones the operator runs by hand when something looks wrong. The warnings can point in two directions—back to the source or away from it—so the operator can narrow down the fault.

sections.title: Measuring Performance
sections.content:
Beyond fault detection, operators need to measure how well the network is performing. Packet loss measurement is tricky in EVPN because multipoint-to-multipoint connectivity means traffic can be delivered to more ports than necessary (e.g., unknown unicast flooding). Instead of counting user data packets, operators use synthetic OAM test packets that are counted only where they should arrive, giving a statistical estimate of real packet loss.

Packet delay and jitter (delay variation) are measured using probes sent through the network. One-way delay measurement requires synchronized clocks between endpoints. Two-way (round-trip) delay can be measured without synchronization. Operators can measure performance either continuously (proactively) or on demand, similar to fault detection.
sections.eli5: Just like you might test your home internet by pinging a server, the network operator sends test packets to measure how fast traffic flows and how consistent the speed is.

sections.title: Connecting Layers
sections.content:
Faults detected in one OAM layer need to be communicated to layers above and below. OAM interworking bridges these gaps. For example, if a link goes down (Link OAM detects it), that alarm should propagate up through Transport OAM and Network OAM to the Service OAM layer, informing the customer-facing monitoring system.

Similarly, when a Network OAM check detects a problem in the EVPN service, it can trigger Service OAM fault notifications. This prevents operators from being flooded with many low-level alarms when a single underlying fault causes multiple service-level failures.
sections.eli5: When a problem is found deep in the network, the operators need to know about it at the top level too. So alerts flow upward to tell the customer-facing system that something is broken.
